rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Aḥsana bī’ differs from ‘aḥsana ilayya’; the former describes beneficence accompanying Yusuf through stages without aiming at his eventual destination.
rows.anchor: فإنه يقال أحسن بي وإلي وهي مختلفة المعاني واليقها بيوسف عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Fī’ is more exact than ‘ʿalā’: the condemned are crucified in the trunks’ middles, whereas ‘ʿalā’ suggests being on top.
rows.anchor: ولم يقل على كما ظن بعضهم لأن على للاستعلاء والمصلوب لا يجعل على رءوس النخل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse says ‘upon it’ rather than ‘in the earth’ because, at annihilation, there is no state of settled permanence or establishment.
rows.anchor: لأن عند الفناء ليس هناك حال القرار والتمكين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believers are temporary sojourners on earth; the arrogant are told not to strut within it, while the humble walk upon it gently.
rows.anchor: قال لا تمش فيها مرحا بل امش عليها هونا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The differing prepositions in ‘believes in God’ and ‘believes the believers’ illustrate that the constructions have distinct meanings.
rows.anchor: وقال تعالى ﴿ يؤمن بالله ويؤمن للمؤمنين ﴾

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās praises God for saying they are heedless of their prayer, rather than heedless within the prayer.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس الحمد الله الذي قال ﴿ عن صلاتهم ساهون ﴾

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī explains that ‘min’ makes the barrier extend from the beginning of the interval to its end, as if it filled all the space between them.
rows.anchor: فلو سقطت من جاز كون الحجاب في الوسط وإن تباعدت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeating the preposition before hearing emphasizes the severity of the sealing in both locations by renewing its grammatical attachment.
rows.anchor: ليكون أدل على شدة الختم في الموضعين حين استجد له تعدية اخرى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hamza is fundamentally interrogative, can seek conceptual identification or assent, and is more frequent than ‘hal’; it uniquely occurs before wāw.
rows.anchor: أصلها الاستفهام وهو طلب الإفهام وتأتي لطلب التصور والتصديق بخلاف هل فإنها للتصور خاصة

words: لمن شاء منكم أن يتقدم أو يتأخر
rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān rejects the rhetoricians’ rule that the object of ‘will’ is omitted unless unexpected, citing verses where it is explicit.
rows.anchor: أنكر الشيخ أبو حيان في باب عوامل الجزم من شرح التسهيل هذه القاعدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The explicit objects do not refute the rule: they name something momentous, which is why they are stated.
rows.anchor: ولهم أن يقولوا إن المفعول هاهنا عظيم فلهذا صرح به فلا غلط على القوم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In ‘mādhā arāda’, either ‘mādhā’ is a fronted relative object, or ‘dhā’ is relative and the object is an omitted pronoun; ‘mathalan’ is circumstantial, not another object.
rows.anchor: فإذا جعلت ماذا بمعنى الذي فمفعول أراد متقدم عليه وإن جعلت ذا وحده بمعنى الذي

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: The object of ‘be patient’ is often omitted, as in the first examples; al-Zamakhsharī says ‘ṣabara ʿan’ omits ‘the self,’ which appears explicitly in 18:28.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري 5 في تفسير سورة الحجرات قولهم صبر عن كذا 6 محذوف منه المفعول وهو النفس

rows.speaker: الفارسي
rows.claim: Al-Fārisī takes ‘yarā’ as governing two omitted objects: seeing the unseen means knowing it, as though the unseen were present; he links this to ‘Knower of the unseen.’
rows.anchor: قال الفارسي الوجه أن يرى هنا للتعدية لمفعولين لأن رؤية الغائب لا تكون إلا علما

rows.speaker: ابن خروف
rows.claim: Ibn Khurūf says the two objects are omitted with contextual evidence: the person knows what he does and believes it true and right.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن خروف هو من باب الحذف لدليل لأن المعنى دال على المفعولين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects the analysis that leaves the objects wholly unspecified: it gives the verse no determinate meaning, despite some scholars adopting it.
rows.anchor: ولا فائدة في الآية مع الاقتصار لأنه لا يعلم منه المراد وقد ذهب إليه بعض المحققين وعدل عن الصواب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Wāʿada’ can take two objects while omitting one; ‘the right side of the Mount’ is the second object, not an adverb, with ‘coming to it’ or ‘staying there’ understood.
rows.anchor: لا يكون ظرفا لاختصاصه والتقدير واعدناكم إتيانه أو مكثا فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Waʿada’ governs two objects and may omit one, like ‘give’ rather than ‘suppose’; ‘jānib’ is the second object, with arrival or stay implied.
rows.anchor: فعل يتعدى لمفعوليين يجوز الاقتصار على احدهما كأعطيته وليس كظننت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because spoils as an abstract event are not literally taken, ‘spoils’ can name the source for its concrete result, or an omitted ‘granting’ can be supplied.
rows.anchor: فالغنيمة تكون الغنم فإن قلت الغنم حدث لا يؤخذ إنما يقع الأخذ على الأعيان دون المعاني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In promises of forgiveness or succession, the prepositional phrase or ‘they will be appointed’ explains the promise rather than serving as a second object, like a clarification of a prior testament.
rows.anchor: فإن الفعل لم يتعد فيه إلى مفعول ثان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In these expressions, the accusative may be a cognate object or a second object; the promised thing can itself be called ‘the promise.’
rows.anchor: فيحتمل انتصاب الواحد بالمصدر أو بأنه المفعول الثاني وسمى الموعود به الوعد كالمخلوق الخلق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘One of the two groups’ is the second object, and ‘that it would be yours’ appositionally explains it; the alternatives are reaching or being granted one group, the caravan or victory.
rows.anchor: و ﴿ إحدى ﴾ في موضع نصب مفعول ثان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the second ‘that’ is appositional, an omitted ‘intending’ must be supplied to complete the clause and make the time phrase a predicate; the alternative parse needs no supplement.
rows.anchor: فمن قدر في أن الثانية البدل فينبغي أن يقدر محذوفا ليتم الكلام فيصح البدل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause describing Abraham’s promise is a genitive adjective of an indefinite noun, with its pronoun returning to that noun; here ‘promise’ takes one object.
rows.anchor: فالجملة في موضع جر صفة للنكرة وقد عاد الضمير فيها إلى الموصوف والفعل متعد إلى واحد

words: أيحب أحدكم أن يأكل لحم أخيه ميتا فكرهتموه
rows.speaker: الفارسي
rows.claim: Al-Fārisī reads ‘you disliked it’ as an answer to the implied ‘no’: just as corpse-eating is disliked, backbiting should be disliked; ‘fear God’ coordinates with an implied command.
rows.anchor: قال الفارسي المعنى فكما كرهتموه فاكرهوا الغيبة

rows.speaker: ابن الشجري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Shajarī finds that parsing far-fetched because it deletes a relative pronoun but leaves its clause; he instead reads ‘so, you have disliked this’ as a new statement, with backbiting likewise disliked.
rows.anchor: قال ابن الشجري وهذا التقدير بعيد لأنه قدر المحذوف موصولا وهو ما المصدرية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qur’anic clauses often omit a verb of saying, so the implied speech is virtually explicit: examples include commands to eat, take, or pray, and greetings spoken by angels.
rows.anchor: أي يقولون ما نعبدهم إلا للقربة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the command to eat manna and quail, an omitted ‘We said’ introduces the speech: ‘We said, eat,’ or ‘saying, eat.’
rows.anchor: أي وقلنا كلوا أو قائلين

words: فمنهم ظالم لنفسه ومنهم مقتصد ومنهم سابق بالخيرات
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Order can follow prevalence: the self-wronging group is named first because it is most numerous, followed by the moderate and then the foremost.
rows.anchor: قدم الظالم لكثرته ثم المقتصد ثم السابق

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī explains that ‘disbeliever’ comes first because most people are not believers, as another verse states, supported also by the hadith about the Fire’s people.
rows.anchor: وجعل منه الزمخشري ﴿ فمنكم كافر ومنكم مؤمن ﴾ 5 يعني بدليل قوله

words: فأما الذين كفروا فأعذبهم عذابا شديدا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Punishment is foregrounded because the address concerns Jews who rejected Jesus and tried to kill him.
rows.anchor: قدم ذكر العذاب لكون الكلام مع اليهود الذين كفروا بعيسى وراموا قتله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The male thief is mentioned first because theft is more frequent among men.
rows.anchor: لأن السرقة في الذكور أكثر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The female adulterer is mentioned first because adultery is more prevalent among women.
rows.anchor: في قوله ﴿ الزانية والزاني ﴾ 9 لأن الزنى فيهن أكثر

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: For the punishment passage, al-Zamakhsharī says the woman is the source of betrayal because her enticement enables the man; for marriage, the man is the suitor and initiator, so he comes first.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري سيقت الآية التي قبلها لعقوبتهما على ما جنيا

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says lowering the gaze comes first because sight leads toward fornication, is more widespread, and is difficult to guard against.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري قدم غض البصر لأن النظر يريد الزنى ورائد الفجور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an generally puts mercy before punishment, matching the divine statement that mercy has preceded wrath.
rows.anchor: ومنه تقديم الرحمة على العذاب حيث وقع في القرآن ولهذا ورد إن رحمتي غلبت غضبي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Māʾida verse reverses the usual order of punishment and forgiveness because its context calls for threat.
rows.anchor: وأما تقديم التعذيب على المغفرة في آية المائدة 7 فللسياق

rows.speaker: ابن الحاجب
rows.claim: Ibn al-Ḥājib explains that wives precede children because enmity is more deeply rooted among spouses; wealth precedes children because it more consistently occasions temptation, as the cited verses illustrate.
rows.anchor: قال ابن الحاجب في أماليه إنما قدم الأزواج لأن المقصود الإخبار أن فيهم أعداء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The usual Qur’anic order names mercy before punishment, in keeping with the report that God’s mercy preceded His wrath.
rows.anchor: من اساليب القرآن حيث ذكر الرحمة والعذاب إن يبدأ بذكر الرحمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The order reverses in the Māʾida passage because it addresses highway robbers and thieves; threat is fitting, and God’s power to enforce it heightens the warning.
rows.anchor: لأنها وردت في ذكر قطاع الطريق والمحاربين والسراق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Punishment precedes mercy in the verse about Abraham because it occurs in his warning to his people.
rows.anchor: لأنها في سياق حكاية إنذار إبراهيم لقومه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The nearby creation and resurrection passage likewise foregrounds warning: it stresses that no protector or helper can save people from God.
rows.anchor: ومثلها ﴿ أو لم يروا كيف يبدئ الله الخلق ثم يعيده إن ذلك على الله يسير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Anʿām ends with punishment first because the sūra repeatedly confronts and threatens disbelievers; the preceding denunciation of sectarian division makes that order apt as a deterrent.
rows.anchor: لأن سورة الانعام كلها مناظرة للكفار ووعيدهم خصوصا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sudden ‘idhā’ is disputed: some restrict it to nominal clauses, while al-Mubarrad and later grammarians treat it as a locative particle marking where an unexpected event is encountered.
rows.anchor: قالوا ولا تقع بعد اذا المفاجأة إلا الجملة الاسمية وبعد اذ إلاالفعل الماضي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pure temporal ‘idhā’ in oaths does not impose a condition: otherwise the oath would occur only when the night fades, whereas the oath is made unconditionally now.
rows.anchor: لأنه لو كان فيها معنى الشرط لكان جوابها معنى ما تقدم ويصير التقدير الاول إذا يغشى أقسم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This ‘idhā’ is purely temporal, since a conditional reading would require a fāʾ in its response.
rows.anchor: لانه لو كان فيها معنى الشرط لوجبت الفاء في جوابها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Conditional ‘idhā’ has a condition and response, commonly with fāʾ; examples include past-form verbs used for future actions and the saying about telling a companion to be quiet.
rows.anchor: والضرب الثاني يقتضي شرطا وجوابا ولهذا تقع الفاء بعدها على حد وقوعها بعد إذ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: According to Sībawayh, conditional ‘idhā’ is not attached directly to a verbal clause; when a noun follows, an omitted verb is estimated, with a nominative noun as its subject.
rows.anchor: ومذهب سيبويه أنها لا تضاف إلى جملة فعلية ولهذا إذا وقع بعدها اسم قدر بينه وبينها فعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When a noun after conditional ‘idhā’ is accusative, the text treats it as the object of an estimated verb, whose subject is also understood, as in the quoted poetry.
rows.anchor: كان مفعولا والفاعل فيه أيضا ذلك المقدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Comparisons may state both subjects explicitly, or leave one implicit in a compact, metaphor-like form, as in the contrast between the two seas.
rows.anchor: قد تشبه أشياء بأشياء ثم تارة يصرح بذكر المشبهات

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī says these are composite parables: separate things can be compared individually, but a whole arrangement is compared with another whole; the second hypocrite parable is more eloquent because it conveys worse confusion and severity.
rows.anchor: قال الزمخشري 4 والذي عليه علماء البيان أن التمثيلين جميعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The most forceful simile omits both the comparison’s aspect and particle; omitting only one yields the less emphatic forms illustrated by ‘Zayd is like a lion.’
rows.anchor: أعلى مراتب التشبيه في الأبلغية ترك وجه الشبه وأداتة نحو زيد أسد

rows.speaker: صاحب المفتاح
rows.claim: The author of al-Miftāḥ implies that dropping the aspect of comparison is more eloquent than dropping its particle because the aspect is more general.
rows.anchor: وفي كلام صاحب المفتاح إشارة إلى أن ترك وجه الشبه أبلغ من ترك أداتة

rows.speaker: صاحب ضوء المصباح
rows.claim: The author of Ḍawʾ al-Miṣbāḥ disagrees: a general omitted aspect may suggest blame rather than praise; the counterargument is that context can also direct an omitted particle toward praise.
rows.anchor: وخالفه صاحب ضوء المصباح 1 لأنه إذا عم واحتمل التعدد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A simile’s particle may attach to an associated circumstance rather than the exact object of comparison, relying on the audience to infer the intended likeness.
rows.anchor: قد تدخل الاداة على شيء وليس هو عين المشبه ولكنه ملتبس به واعتمد على فهم المخاطب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an uses plural, dual, or singular forms for east and west according to context; the dual can denote the sun’s rising and setting extremes as it travels seasonally.
rows.anchor: ومنها مجىء المشرق والمغرب في القرآن تارة بالجمع وأخرى بالتثنية وأخرى بالإفراد

words: لا الشمس ينبغي لها أن تدرك القمر
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation invokes continuous celestial motions, whose courses cannot be reduced to a fixed measurement; the sun’s and moon’s rising and setting points shift through the seasons.
rows.anchor: وقيل هو إخبار عن الحركات الفلكية متحركة بحركات متداركة لا تنضبط لخطة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Singular ‘east and west’ names each direction without counting its many rising and setting points; plural counts individual points, while dual groups the seasonal ranges into two.
rows.anchor: فحيث أفرد الله له لفظ المشرق والمغرب أراد به الجهة نفسها التى تشتمل الواحدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation says the basmala was omitted because Arabs announcing treaty annulment sent the notice without it, and the Prophet followed that custom when reciting the sūra.
rows.anchor: إذا كان بينهم وبين قوم عهد وأرادوا نقضه كتبوا لهم كتابا ولم يكتبوا فيه

rows.speaker: عثمان
rows.claim: In a report cited from al-Ḥākim’s Ṣaḥīḥ, ʿUthmān says al-Anfāl was early and Barāʾa late; their similar subject and the Prophet’s lack of clarification led them to think they were one sūra, so he left no basmala between them.
rows.anchor: في صحيح الحاكم أن عثمان رضي الله عنه قال كانت الأنفال من أوائل ما نزل

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Mālik’s explanation is that when the beginning of the sūra was omitted, its basmala was omitted with it.
rows.anchor: وعن مالك أن أولها لما سقط سقطت البسملة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reported explanation is that Barāʾa was as long as al-Baqara.
rows.anchor: وقد قيل إنها كانت تعدل البقرة لطولها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further explanation says the compilers disagreed whether al-Anfāl and Barāʾa were one sūra or two, and therefore omitted the basmala between them.
rows.anchor: وقيل لأنه لما كتبوا المصاحف فى زمن عثمان اختلفوا هل هما سورتان

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: When Ibn ʿAbbās asked him, ʿAlī explained that the basmala signifies security, while Barāʾa came with the sword and contains no security.
rows.anchor: وفي مستدرك الحاكم أيضا عن ابن عباس سألت عليا عن ذلك فقال لأن البسملة أمان

rows.speaker: القشيري
rows.claim: Al-Qushayrī calls the correct explanation that the basmala was absent because Gabriel did not reveal it with this sūra.
rows.anchor: قال القشيري والصحيح أن البسملة لم تكن فيها لأن جبريل عليه السلام ما نزل بها فيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This reverses the expected simile: although the debate concerns usury, its advocates make usury the norm and assimilate trade to it, pressing for usury’s permissibility.
rows.anchor: كان الأصل أن يقولوا إنما الربا مثل البيع لأن الكلام في الربا لا في البيع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second reading sees a dialectical challenge: if excess makes usury forbidden, trade could also be forbidden by analogy; the Qur’anic answer breaks that proposed link, distinguishes God’s rulings, and rejects analogy against revelation.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن يكون المراد إلزام الإسلام فيحرم البيع قياسا على الربا لاشتماله على الفضل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reversed question confronts idolaters on their own terms: since they elevate non-creators as gods, it applies the stronger argument by lowering the sacred Creator rather than raising the deficient idols.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أنهم لما قاسوا غير الخالق خوطبوا بأشد الإلزامين وهو تنقيص المقدس

rows.speaker: السكاكي
rows.claim: Al-Sakkākī says ‘who does not create’ means a living, capable creator, indirectly rejecting any comparison between idols and God a fortiori.
rows.anchor: قال السكاكي وعندي أن المراد ب من لا يخلق الحي القادر من الخلق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The syntax makes desire stronger and more binding for the person than his supposed deity by placing desire in the position of the god.
rows.anchor: فإنه جعل المفعول الأول ثانيا والثاني أولا للتنبيه على أن الهوى أقوى وأوثق عنده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author lists the question of equating Muslims with criminals as another example in this discussion of rhetorical inversion.
rows.anchor: ومنه قوله تعالى ﴿ أفنجعل المسلمين كالمجرمين ﴾

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Abraham’s rejection of setting stars supports the Prophet’s report that the source of fitna and disbelief is toward the east; repentance’s door opens from the west.
rows.anchor: ما يبين تصديق النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم في قوله رأس الفتنة والكفر نحو المشرق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening of revelation is linked to the Qur’anic announcement that God’s command has come and that angels bring revelation to chosen servants.
rows.anchor: ومن ذلك بدء الوحى فى قوله سبحانه

rows.speaker: خديجة
rows.claim: Khadīja reassured the Prophet at the start of revelation that God would never disgrace him because he maintained kinship ties.
rows.anchor: وقول خديجة والله لا يخزيك الله أبدا إنك لتصل الرحم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people’s request for Moses’ prayer and Jonah’s deliverance are connected with teachings about divine relief, followed by the cave companions’ appeal through their best deeds.
rows.anchor: وفى هذا بين صلى الله عليه وسلم أصحاب الغار الثلاثة

rows.speaker: أصحاب الغار
rows.claim: The three people trapped in the cave advised one another to pray to God by each person’s best deed, hoping for release.
rows.anchor: وفى هذا بين صلى الله عليه وسلم أصحاب الغار الثلاثة إذ قال بعضهم لبعض ليدع كل واحد

rows.speaker: ورقة
rows.claim: Waraqa wished he would live to see the Prophet expelled by his people; Qur’anic threats against Shuʿayb and earlier messengers echo that prediction.
rows.anchor: وقول ورقة ياليتنى حي إذ يخرجك قومك إلخ

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet said every messenger bringing his message faced hostility; the sūra confirms that earlier peoples likewise called messengers sorcerers or madmen.
rows.anchor: وكذلك قوله لم يأت أحد بما جئت به إلا عودى من قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Night Journey report is corroborated by Sūrat al-Isrāʾ and the opening of Sūrat al-Najm.
rows.anchor: ومن ذلك حديث المعراج مصداقه فى سورة الإسراء وفى صدر سورة النجم

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet said he most resembled Abraham’s son, and the author links that report to the command that the Prophet follow Abraham’s upright way.
rows.anchor: وقوله صلى الله عليه وسلم رأيت إبراهيم وأنا أشبه ولده به من مفهوم قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says prophetic words come true in history and divine decree; recitation and reflection disclose their truth, while Jesus, as a divine Word, arrives at judgment purified of sin.
rows.anchor: وهكذا حاله حيث جاءت صدقا وعدلا فتطلب صدق كلماته بترداد تلاوتك لكتابه ونظرك في مصنوعاته

rows.speaker: ابن مالك
rows.claim: Ibn Mālik treats the hadith’s ‘there is no prayer more burdensome’ as evidence that ‘laysa’ can negate the entire genus, not merely one instance.
rows.anchor: غير ابن مالك في كتاب شواهد التوضيح فقال في قوله صلى الله عليه وسلم ليس صلاة اثقل على المنافقين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage explains ‘min ladun’ as ‘from/at,’ more specific than ‘ʿinda’ because it marks the point where an interval begins.
rows.anchor: بمعنى عند وهي أخص منها لدلالته على ابتدائها به نحو أقمت عنده من لدن طلوع الشمس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Min ladun’ marks a starting point and can make the endpoint of an action clearer than ‘ʿinda’; several verses illustrate its uses.
rows.anchor: فتوضح نهاية الفعل وهي ابلغ من عند

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The nūn in ‘ladun’ can be dropped, as in the forms ‘ladā’ and ‘ladayya’ in the cited verses.
rows.anchor: وقد تحذف نونها قال تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ‘Mā’ has twelve uses, six nominal and six particles; nominal ‘mā’ is definite if replaceable by ‘alladhī’ and indefinite if replaceable by ‘shayʾ,’ with some examples allowing either.
rows.anchor: فالاسمية ضربان معرفة ونكرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Relative ‘mā’ does not change for masculine or feminine, singular, dual, or plural; its referent determines whether it means ‘alladhī’ or ‘allatī.’
rows.anchor: فالأول من الستة الاسماء الخبرية وهي الموصولة ويستوي فيها التذكير والتانيث والافراد والتثنية والجمع

rows.speaker: السهيلي
rows.claim: Al-Suhaylī rejects the claim that relative ‘mā’ simply equals ‘alladhī’: ‘mā’ is more ambiguous and can refer even to what does not exist.
rows.anchor: وقال السهيلي كذا يقول النحويون انها بمعنى الذي مطلقا وليس كذلك بل بينهما تخالف
